### 1. Introduction
Chronic kidney disease (CKD), a major global health burden, is defined as kidney damage or a glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 for three months or more, irrespective of cause [ 1 ]. It is characterized by a progressive decline in kidney function, leading to the accumulation of toxins and metabolic waste in the body, and may ultimately progress to end-stage renal disease (ESRD). According to epidemiological data, the global prevalence of CKD is approximately 9.5% [ 2 ]. Mounting evidence indicates that CKD is associated not only with impaired renal filtration but also with abnormal lipid metabolism, activation of inflammatory pathways, and elevated oxidative stress [ 3–5 ]. Consequently, patients with CKD frequently develop coronary artery disease (CAD), a narrowing or blockage of the coronary arteries, typically due to the buildup of plaque [ 6 ], which results in a markedly increased risk of cardiovascular events, particularly among those with advanced renal impairment. The mortality from heart disease is substantially higher in individuals with CKD than in those without renal dysfunction [ 7 ]. Moreover, CKD is recognized as an independent predictor of poor prognosis in CAD [ 8 ], while CAD, primarily caused by atherosclerosis of the coronary arteries, leads to myocardial ischemia and is a major contributor to myocardial infarction and heart failure. Studies have identified CAD as the leading single cause of death worldwide [ 9 ]. The high comorbidity rate and the complex, bidirectional interactions between these two diseases are particularly noteworthy [ 10 ]. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying CKD-CAD comorbidity remain complex and incompletely understood. Thus, investigating the pathogenic link between CKD and CAD holds substantial clinical significance. Against this backdrop, artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) technologies offer powerful tools for deciphering the complex mechanisms underlying CKD-CAD c

### 2.1. Experimental design and data sources
The GWAS summary statistics for CKD were obtained from the CKDGen consortium ( https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gwas/ ), comprising a sample of 452,264 individuals of European ancestry [ 23 ]. The chronic kidney disease (CKD) GWAS summary statistics were obtained from the CKDGen consortium, which primarily includes individuals with mild to moderate CKD stages and explicitly excludes end-stage renal disease (ESRD) or dialysis patients. Summary-level data for coronary artery disease (CAD) were retrieved from the IEU Open GWAS database ( https://gwas.mrcieu.ac.uk ), accession number ebi-a-GCST005195, comprising 122,733 CAD cases and 424,528 controls [ 24 ]. This case includes a composite endpoint of myocardial infarction, stable or unstable angina, and significant stenosis confirmed by coronary angiography. In addition, cis-pQTLs were defined as single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) located within 1 Mb of the gene encoding the corresponding plasma protein. The pQTL dataset was derived from the DECODE database ( https://www.decode.com/ ) based on the 2021 study by Ferkingstad et al. which included 35,559 participants and quantified 4907 plasma proteins [ 25 ]. Gene expression data were downloaded from the GEO database. GSE113079 ( https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE113079 ) contained blood microarray data from 93 patients with CAD and 48 healthy controls (CTLs), generated using the GPL20115 platform. GSE66494 ( https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE66494 ) included blood microarray data from 53 patients with CKD and 8 CTLs, profiled on the GPL6480 platform ( https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/ ) [ 26 ] ( Table 1 , Supplemental Table S1 ).

### 2.8. Justification for threshold selection methods in the analysis
2.8.1. Differentially Expressed Gene (DEG) cutoff: |log 2 FC| &gt; 0.263
The threshold of |log 2 FC| &gt; 0.263 (corresponding to a |FC| ≥ 1.2) for screening differentially expressed genes (DEGs) was selected based on biological rationale and field consensus. This cutoff aims to balance sensitivity and specificity, enabling the capture of subtle yet stable expression changes while avoiding the omission of key signals with an overly high threshold or the introduction of noise with an overly low one. This specific threshold was successfully applied in the study by Ren et al. [ 43 ], where they used this criterion, combined with an adjusted p-value &lt; 0.05, to identify 831 DEGs and construct a high-accuracy diagnostic model for ischemic stroke (AUC 0.81–0.933), thereby validating its reliability. In the current cardiorenal syndrome study, adopting this same threshold ensures comparability with published literature and helps focus on functionally relevant genes (e.g. those involved in inflammation and fibrosis pathways). This supports subsequent machine learning and pathway analyses, enhancing the study’s rigor and interpretability. 2.8.2. DALEX feature importance threshold: Top 20%
Selecting the top 20% of features based on importance scores calculated using the DALEXpackage is a widely adopted strategy in interpretable machine learning to balance model performance, complexity, and interpretability. DALEX uses permutation importance, where the contribution of each feature is estimated by measuring the drop in model performance (e.g. accuracy) when its values are randomly shuffled. A larger drop indicates greater feature importance. The top 20% cutoff enables the model to retain its most influential predictors while reducing data dimensionality, filtering out redundant or noisy variables, and improving both interpretability and computational efficiency. Relative importance ranking is generally more stable than absolute importance values, especially in high-dimensional

### 3.1. MR analysis of CKD and CAD
Using 891 stringently selected genetic IVs ( p &lt; 5 × 10 −8 , kb &gt; 10,000, and r 2 &lt; 0.001), MR analysis demonstrated that CKD is associated with an elevated risk of CAD (OR = 1.04, 95% CI: 1.033–1.047) ( Figure 2(A) ). Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of the causal inference, indicating no heterogeneity (Q test, p = 1.000), no evidence of horizontal pleiotropy (MR-Egger intercept, p = 0.750), and a well-supported causal directionality (Steiger test, p &lt; 1 × 10–15). In contrast, reverse MR analysis, conducted using 126 harmonized SNPs, showed no evidence of a causal effect of CAD on CKD (OR = 0.999, 95% CI: 0.962–1.037) ( Figure 2(B) ). All supporting figures and tables are available in the supplementary materials (Figure S1; Table S2 ).

### 3.2. Shared DEGs between CKD and CAD
Differential expression analysis of CAD versus CTL samples identified 7,326 DEGs based on thresholds of p &lt; 0.05 and |log 2 FC| &gt; 0.263 [ 43 ]. Among these, 3,404 genes were upregulated, and 3,922 were downregulated in CAD ( Figure 3(A,B) ). Similarly, comparison between CKD and CTL samples yielded 6,095 DEGs, including 4,709 upregulated and 1,386 downregulated genes ( Figure 3(C,D) ). Intersection analysis of upregulated and downregulated DEGs across both diseases identified 3,906 shared DEGs, suggesting overlapping molecular signatures that may underlie the comorbidity of CKD and CAD ( Figure 3(E) ).

### 3.3. MR analysis of shared plasma protein pQTLs and CAD
By intersecting the plasma proteins corresponding to the shared DEGs, a total of 230 proteins related to CKD–CAD comorbidity were identified ( Figure 4(A) ). A total of 9,053 SNPs were selected based on pQTL data from the DECODE database ( p &lt; 5 × 10 −8 , kb &gt; 10,000, and r 2 &lt; 0.001). After harmonization using the harmonise_data function, 5,864 valid IVs were retained. MR analysis identified 25 plasma proteins with a genetically causal association with CAD ( Figure 4(B,C) ). After sensitivity analysis, 15 proteins were retained as genetically causal candidates for CAD ( Figure 4(B,C) ). The robustness of these causal associations was supported by sensitivity analyses, which revealed no evidence of heterogeneity (Q test, p &gt; 0.05), no horizontal pleiotropy (MR-Egger intercept and MR-PRESSO global test, p &gt; 0.05), and strong support for causal directionality based on the Steiger test ( p &lt; 1 × 10 −10 ) ( Table 2 ). Furthermore, the scatter plot showed intercepts of IVs close to zero, and the funnel plot appeared symmetric without outliers, indicating minimal bias among the instruments ( Figure 4(D) ; Supplemental Figs. S2–S26 ).
Venn and forest plots identifying 15 CAD-linked proteins via pQTL-MR, plus funnel plots for sensitivity analysis. Table 2.
Mendelian randomization estimates identifying plasma proteins genetically causally linked to coronary artery disease in CKD–CAD comorbidity.

### 3.4. Functional enrichment analysis and PPI network of core proteins
GO enrichment analysis revealed that the 15 proteins were significantly associated with 208 functional terms (FDR &lt; 0.05), including 174 under the biological process category. Key enriched terms included the regulation of the smoothened signaling pathway ( Figure 5(A–D) ; Supplemental Figs. S27 –29). KEGG pathway analysis further revealed that these proteins were collectively involved in seven critical signaling pathways ( Figure 5(E) ; Figure S30; Table S3 ). PPI analysis, performed using a confidence threshold of 0.1, identified interaction pairs among 10 of the 15 proteins. The resulting interaction network, visualized using Cytoscape (version 3.8.2) ( Figure 5(F) ), highlighted HGF and SERPINE2 as nodes with the highest degree centrality, underscoring their potential regulatory importance within the network. Functional annotation showed that these proteins were predominantly enriched in signaling pathways associated with organ development and pathophysiological processes involving coagulation and fibrosis. Notably, the HGF-SERPINE2 interaction hub appeared to serve as a central mediator in the progression of cardiorenal fibrosis. Overall, the enriched pathways were organized into two major functional clusters: (1) developmental pathways involved in angiogenesis and tissue morphogenesis, and (2) pathological pathways associated with thrombosis, inflammatory responses, and fibrotic remodeling.

### 3.5. Selection and evaluation of diagnostic proteins
Candidate diagnostic proteins were identified via cross-validation using the Boruta algorithm and an SVM model with a radial basis function (SVM-RBF) in independent CAD and CKD cohorts ( Figure 6 ). A five-fold cross-validation strategy was employed, wherein the dataset was randomly divided into five equal subsets. During each iteration, four subsets were used for model training and one for validation, such that each subset served once as the validation set. The final performance was calculated as the average of all five validation results. Based on this strategy, six robust diagnostic biomarkers were identified: LIMA1, PLCG1, HGF, PZP, SERPINE2, and TXNDC15. Based on its suboptimal performance (AUC = 0.685, below the 0.7 threshold) in the CAD cohort, SPINT2 was excluded from the final diagnostic panel. This decision was based strictly on the pre-defined performance threshold. In the CAD cohort, the AUC values of the selected proteins ranged from 0.759 (LIMA1, PLCG1, TXNDC15) to 0.804 (SERPINE2). In contrast, the CKD cohort demonstrated markedly higher predictive performance, with AUC values ranging from 0.887 (SERPINE2) to 0.995 (PLCG1), the latter indicating near-perfect diagnostic accuracy ( Table 4 ). A nomogram model constructed using these six biomarkers ( Figure 7 ) enabled quantitative estimation of disease risk. For instance, a total score of 392 corresponded to a 99.9% probability of CAD, whereas a score of 305 corresponded to an approximately 100% probability of CKD. This model offers a clinically applicable tool for visualizing individual risk and facilitating early diagnosis.
ML selection of six plasma biomarkers for CKD–CAD diagnosis using Boruta and SVM-RBF. Table 4.

### 3.6. MR analysis of CKD–diagnostic protein pQTLs
MR analysis demonstrated robust causal associations between genetically predicted CKD and six plasma diagnostic proteins: LIMA1 (OR = 1.065, 95% CI: 1.058–1.072), PZP (OR = 1.053, 95% CI: 1.046–1.061), and PLCG1 (OR = 1.046, 95% CI: 1.040–1.053) were identified as genetic risk factors for CAD; whereas SERPINE2 (OR = 0.99, 95% CI: 0.983–0.998), TXNDC15 (OR = 0.98, 95% CI: 0.973–0.986), and HGF (OR = 0.956, 95% CI: 0.950–0.960) acted as protective factors ( Figure 8(A) ). Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of these findings, indicating no significant heterogeneity (Cochran’s Q test, p &gt; 0.05), no evidence of horizontal pleiotropy (MR-Egger and MR-PRESSO tests, p &gt; 0.05), and no directional bias (Steiger test, p &lt; 1 × 10 −10 ). The validity of IVs was further supported by scatter plots and funnel plots ( Supplemental Figs. S31 –36; Table S4 ). Mediation analysis revealed that LIMA1, PZP, and PLCG1 mediated the positive causal effect of CKD on CAD, while HGF, SERPINE2, and TXNDC15 mediated protective effects, collectively constituting the causal pathway of “CKD–plasma protein–CAD” ( Figure 8(B) ; Table 3 ).
Mediation analysis of plasma proteins in CKD-to-CAD progression. Table 3.

### 3.7. Construction of the GeneMANIA network and functional prediction of diagnostic proteins
A co-expression network comprising the six diagnostic proteins was generated using the GeneMANIA platform ( http://genemania.org/ ), which revealed significant interactions within pathways among these proteins ( Figure 9(A) ). Functional enrichment analysis showed that the diagnostic proteins and their interactors were collectively involved in biological processes such as regulation of cholesterol metabolic process, extrinsic component of plasma membrane, sterol biosynthetic process, host interaction, and regulation of alcohol/steroid biosynthetic processes ( Figure 9(B) ).
GeneMANIA network and function treemap of six core plasma proteins in sterol/lipid metabolism. GSEA further highlighted the regulation of several key biological pathways by these diagnostic proteins ( Figure 10 ; Supplemental Figs. S37–38 ).

### 3.8. ssGSEA of immune infiltration and diagnostic proteins
The ssGSEA of immune infiltration revealed distinct immune landscape alterations in both CAD and CKD. In CAD, seven pro-inflammatory immune cell populations, including dendritic cells (DCs), macrophages, and neutrophils, exhibited significantly increased infiltration scores ( p &lt; 0.01), whereas ten lymphocyte subsets, such as CD8 + T cells and cytotoxic cells, showed decreased infiltration scores ( Figure 11(A) . In contrast, the CKD cohort showed significantly decreased infiltration scores in twelve immune cell types, including cytotoxic cells and natural killer (NK) cells ( Figure 11(B) . Correlation analysis between key diagnostic proteins and immune cell abundance indicated disease-specific immune associations. Within the CAD microenvironment, HGF expression correlated positively with macrophages and neutrophils ( r &gt; 0.5) and negatively with CD8 + T cells (r &lt; −0.4); PLCG1 correlated positively with CD8 + T cells ( r = 0.42) and negatively with DCs (r = −0.38); PZP showed a significant negative correlation with macrophages (r = −0.61) ( Figures 11C ; Supplemental Figs. S39 –44). Within the CKD microenvironment, HGF, LIMA1, and SERPINE2 were negatively correlated with NK cells (r &lt; −0.6), while PZP correlated positively with effector memory T cells (Tem) ( r = 0.53) ( Figs 11D ; Supplemental Figs. S45 –50).

### 3.9. Drug–protein interaction prediction and molecular docking of diagnostic proteins
Potential drug–protein interactions were predicted using the DGIdb, which identified multiple drugs targeting HGF, PLCG1, and PZP ( Table 5 , Figure 12(A) ). Among these, compounds with the highest “interaction_group_score” were selected for molecular docking analyses. The three-dimensional crystal structures of the proteins and the corresponding small-molecule ligands were obtained for docking simulations ( Table 6 ). The docking results demonstrated stable interactions between the selected compounds and their protein targets. In HGF, three amino acid residues—TYR-369, ARG-331, and SER-378—formed hydrogen bonds with imatinib mesylate, yielding a docking affinity of −9.7 kcal/mol ( Figure 12(B) ). In PLCG1, three residues (GLN-659, GLU-548, SER-665) formed hydrogen bonds with phosphomethylphosphonic acid adenosyl ester, resulting in a docking affinity of −6.7 kcal/mol ( Figure 12(C) ). For PZP, two residues (SER-92, ASN-41) formed hydrogen bonds with norethindrone, with a docking affinity of −8.3 kcal/mol ( Figure 12(D) ). These docking interactions suggest that HGF, PLCG1, and PZP may serve as potential therapeutic targets for pharmacological modulation in cardiorenal comorbidity, warranting further experimental validation.

### 4.1. Background and pathogenic mechanisms of the lipid-inflammation axis
Recent advances in microarray and high-throughput sequencing technologies have markedly enhanced the understanding of molecular features and pathogenic mechanisms underlying complex diseases [ 46 , 47 ]. Meanwhile, the integration of bioinformatics with machine learning has become an increasingly powerful strategy for identifying novel pathogenic genes, diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers, elucidating disease mechanisms, and guiding targeted therapeutic development [ 48 , 49 ].
The lipid-inflammation axis serves as a critical bridge in the comorbidity of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and coronary artery disease (CAD). This bidirectional pathogenic loop arises from the interplay between lipid metabolism disorders and chronic inflammation, which together exacerbate cardiorenal injury. In CKD, impaired renal function leads to defective lipid clearance, causing elevated triglycerides, reduced high-density lipoprotein (HDL) levels, and accumulation of atherogenic low-density lipoprotein (LDL) particles [ 50 ]. These dyslipidemic changes promote lipid deposition in renal and vascular tissues, triggering lipotoxic injury and macrophage activation, with subsequent overproduction of inflammatory mediators like IL-6 and TNF-α [ 51 ]. Inflammation further amplifies lipid abnormalities by impairing lipoprotein metabolism and increasing oxidized lipid species [ 52 ]. Clinical evidence highlights biomarkers such as oxidized LDL and hs-CRP for early risk identification [ 53 ]. Therapeutic strategies like statins, which combine lipid-lowering and anti-inflammatory effects, target this axis [ 54 ]. CAD exacerbates the pathology through ischemia-induced hypoxia, activating RAAS and sympathetic pathways, which promote vasoconstriction and oxidative stress, advancing renal fibrosis and atherosclerosis [ 55 ]. This creates a positive feedback loop, where CAD-related hypoxia worsens lipid-inflammation dysregulation, accelerating CKD progression [ 56 ]. Thus, the axis integrates hemodynam

### 4.3. Clinical implications and therapeutic potential
The clinical management of CAD in patients with CKD has long been constrained by diagnostic and therapeutic limitations. Diagnostic approaches have traditionally relied on single indicators—such as eGFR to assess renal function or coronary artery calcium scoring to evaluate vascular lesions [ 57 ], while treatment strategies have primarily focused on non-organ-specific interventions, such as lipid-lowering statins [ 58 ]. This compartmentalized approach overlooks the shared pathophysiological mechanisms underpinning cardiorenal interactions, leading to inadequate risk stratification and delayed therapeutic intervention. Furthermore, therapeutic choices remain limited for patients with advanced CKD, who are frequently excluded from major cardiovascular outcome trials. As a result, cardiovascular management in CKD is often extrapolated from non-CKD populations, diminishing its clinical applicability [ 59 ]. By integrating transcriptomic and plasma proteomic genetic data, this study provides a novel MR-validated multi-protein biomarker signature involving a six-protein panel (LIMA1, PLCG1, HGF, PZP, SERPINE2, and TXNDC15) with robust diagnostic potential. Machine learning–based feature selection validated its strong discriminative capacity in both CAD (AUC = 0.759–0.804) and CKD (AUC = 0.887–0.995) cohorts. This plasma protein panel represents a shift from isolated organ assessment toward a coordinated, multi-target diagnostic strategy. The use of quantifiable circulating biomarkers offers a more comprehensive and biologically grounded approach for the early identification of individuals at high risk of developing cardiorenal comorbidity.
Dyslipidemia has long been recognized as a shared risk factor for both CAD and CKD [ 60 ]. Therapeutic strategies targeting lipid metabolism have dual benefits in cardiorenal comorbidities: statins not only reduce the risk of cardiovascular events in CKD patients but also improve renal function [ 61 ]; combination therapy with statins

### 4.4. The regulatory role of macrophage polarization and immune microenvironment in cardiorenal comorbidity
For decades, macrophage polarization has been recognized as a key determinant in the pathogenesis of both CKD and CAD. In CKD, infiltrating M1-type macrophages promote renal interstitial fibrosis by releasing pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-1β, while M2-type macrophages contribute to tissue repair—an established concept supported by numerous studies [ 66 , 67 ]. Similarly, earlier studies on CAD have reported highly similar mechanisms, suggesting that macrophage dysfunction may disrupt immune tolerance in CAD patients, thereby accelerating disease progression. Modulating macrophage polarization from the pro-inflammatory M1 phenotype to the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype has been shown to improve cardiovascular health and mitigate the development of atherosclerosis [ 68 ]. This cross-organ paradigm of macrophage polarization thus provides mechanistic support for the proposed “cardiorenal lipid-inflammation axis.” In this study, immune infiltration analysis revealed potential protein-mediated modulation of macrophage functional plasticity. In the CAD group ( Figure 11(A /C)), macrophage infiltration scores were significantly increased and positively correlated with HGF, SERPINE2, and TXNDC15 ( r &gt; 0), suggesting that these proteins may promote macrophage activation. Conversely, macrophage scores exhibited significant negative correlations with PLCG1 and PZP ( r &lt; 0), implying suppressive effects on macrophage activity.

### 4.5. Mechanisms and therapeutic implications of core plasma proteins mediating cardiorenal comorbidity via modulation of the lipid-inflammation axis
Notably, the known role of LIMA1 in intestinal cholesterol absorption [ 76 ] aligns with our findings on its regulatory function in lipid metabolism, thus further supporting the central role of lipid dysregulation in cardiorenal disease. Based on these insights, we propose that targeting the lipid–inflammation axis (for instance, modulating LIMA1-mediated cholesterol metabolism) may serve as a novel therapeutic strategy for simultaneously mitigating cardiac and renal injury. This approach not only builds on the established clinical benefits of lipid-lowering therapy but also provides a mechanistic foundation for the development of precision-targeted interventions in cardiorenal syndrome.
As a multi-domain protein activated through proteolytic cleavage, HGF regulates critical processes, including cell migration, proliferation, and apoptosis. In response to tissue injury, upregulated HGF expression activates anti-apoptotic pathways, promotes angiogenesis, and enhances the secretion of the anti-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-10 (IL-10). Upon binding to its receptor Met, HGF exerts cardioprotective effects by inhibiting hypoxia-induced autophagy and has been identified as a potential biomarker for cardiovascular diseases [ 77–79 ]. In this study, MR analysis confirmed that HGF may serve as an endogenous protective factor that mitigates both renal and cardiovascular injury. GSEA revealed significant activation of lysosomal function and autophagy regulatory pathways in CAD patients with high HGF expression ( Figure 10(a) ). These results are consistent with previous reports demonstrating that HGF prevents autophagic cell death and maintains cardiomyocyte homeostasis via the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway [ 80 ]. Remarkably, this study uncovers a novel bidirectional regulatory role of HGF in the cardiorenal system. In the CKD cohort, HGF significantly activated ferroptosis pathways ( Figure 10(b) ), which could be interpreted as evidence of a potential link to lipid peroxid

### 4.6. Methodological comparison and positioning: the relationship between this study and previous Mendelian randomization-machine learning research in the field of cardiorenal disease
The research paradigm integrating Mendelian randomization and machine learning employed in this study is highly consistent with recent trends in biomarker discovery for cardiovascular and renal diseases published in top-tier international journals, while providing distinctive refinement for the complex disease model of cardiorenal comorbidity. For instance, a landmark 2024 study published in European Heart Journal (IF = 37.6) systematically analyzed the associations between 259 plasma proteins and myocardial infarction (MI) risk using large-scale cohorts and a two-sample MR approach, successfully identifying 45 associated proteins and specifically revealing significant sex-specific differences in 13 of them, with stronger associations in women [ 94 ]. Furthermore, a systematic study published in Protein &amp; Cell (IF = 12.8) in 2025 analyzed 14-year follow-up data from 53,026 participants, linked 2,920 plasma proteins to 14 cardiovascular disease outcomes, and through machine learning models and two-sample MR analysis, not only screened high-performance predictive biomarkers but also validated their causal relationship with the diseases, providing crucial evidence for precise early warning [ 95 ]. In the field of kidney disease, a study published in Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism (IF = 5.7) integrated machine learning, MR, and mediation analysis to successfully pinpoint key genes for diabetic kidney disease and elucidated their mechanism of influencing disease progression by regulating pathways such as renal fibrosis and inflammation, demonstrating the depth of this method in deciphering complex kidney pathologies [ 96 ].

### 4.7. Novelty and future applications
The core innovation of this study lies in the identification and validation of a specific combination of six proteins, which may provide a precise tool for risk assessment of cardiorenal comorbidity that is potentially superior to traditional clinical indicators [ 97 ]. At the translational application level, this protein signature can be further developed as a key component of a polygenic risk scoring system; research indicates that integrating proteomic information with genetic risk data can significantly enhance the identification of high-risk populations for cardiovascular events and renal function progression [ 98–99 ]. A dynamic risk stratification model constructed based on this score could enable precise recommendations for personalized screening initiation times and monitoring frequencies for patients at different risk levels, thereby optimizing the allocation of clinical resources [ 100 ]. More importantly, as key mediators of specific pathophysiological pathways, these proteins can be directly incorporated into drug screening pipelines. For instance, levels of proteins such as hepatocyte growth factor are significantly associated with cardiovascular mortality risk, providing direction for rapidly identifying candidate compounds that can modulate these targets and opening new avenues for developing targeted therapies and individualized treatment strategies for cardiorenal comorbidity [ 101 ].

### 1. Introduction
Chronic kidney disease (CKD), a major global health burden, is defined as kidney damage or a glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 for three months or more, irrespective of cause [ 1 ]. It is characterized by a progressive decline in kidney function, leading to the accumulation of toxins and metabolic waste in the body, and may ultimately progress to end-stage renal disease (ESRD). According to epidemiological data, the global prevalence of CKD is approximately 9.5% [ 2 ]. Mounting evidence indicates that CKD is associated not only with impaired renal filtration but also with abnormal lipid metabolism, activation of inflammatory pathways, and elevated oxidative stress [ 3–5 ]. Consequently, patients with CKD frequently develop coronary artery disease (CAD), a narrowing or blockage of the coronary arteries, typically due to the buildup of plaque [ 6 ], which results in a markedly increased risk of cardiovascular events, particularly among those with advanced renal impairment. The mortality from heart disease is substantially higher in individuals with CKD than in those without renal dysfunction [ 7 ]. Moreover, CKD is recognized as an independent predictor of poor prognosis in CAD [ 8 ], while CAD, primarily caused by atherosclerosis of the coronary arteries, leads to myocardial ischemia and is a major contributor to myocardial infarction and heart failure. Studies have identified CAD as the leading single cause of death worldwide [ 9 ]. The high comorbidity rate and the complex, bidirectional interactions between these two diseases are particularly noteworthy [ 10 ]. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying CKD-CAD comorbidity remain complex and incompletely understood. Thus, investigating the pathogenic link between CKD and CAD holds substantial clinical significance. Against this backdrop, artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) technologies offer powerful tools for deciphering the complex mechanisms underlying CKD-CAD c

### 2.1. Experimental design and data sources
The GWAS summary statistics for CKD were obtained from the CKDGen consortium ( https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gwas/ ), comprising a sample of 452,264 individuals of European ancestry [ 23 ]. The chronic kidney disease (CKD) GWAS summary statistics were obtained from the CKDGen consortium, which primarily includes individuals with mild to moderate CKD stages and explicitly excludes end-stage renal disease (ESRD) or dialysis patients. Summary-level data for coronary artery disease (CAD) were retrieved from the IEU Open GWAS database ( https://gwas.mrcieu.ac.uk ), accession number ebi-a-GCST005195, comprising 122,733 CAD cases and 424,528 controls [ 24 ]. This case includes a composite endpoint of myocardial infarction, stable or unstable angina, and significant stenosis confirmed by coronary angiography. In addition, cis-pQTLs were defined as single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) located within 1 Mb of the gene encoding the corresponding plasma protein. The pQTL dataset was derived from the DECODE database ( https://www.decode.com/ ) based on the 2021 study by Ferkingstad et al. which included 35,559 participants and quantified 4907 plasma proteins [ 25 ]. Gene expression data were downloaded from the GEO database. GSE113079 ( https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE113079 ) contained blood microarray data from 93 patients with CAD and 48 healthy controls (CTLs), generated using the GPL20115 platform. GSE66494 ( https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE66494 ) included blood microarray data from 53 patients with CKD and 8 CTLs, profiled on the GPL6480 platform ( https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/ ) [ 26 ] ( Table 1 , Supplemental Table S1 ).

### 2.8. Justification for threshold selection methods in the analysis
2.8.1. Differentially Expressed Gene (DEG) cutoff: |log 2 FC| &gt; 0.263
The threshold of |log 2 FC| &gt; 0.263 (corresponding to a |FC| ≥ 1.2) for screening differentially expressed genes (DEGs) was selected based on biological rationale and field consensus. This cutoff aims to balance sensitivity and specificity, enabling the capture of subtle yet stable expression changes while avoiding the omission of key signals with an overly high threshold or the introduction of noise with an overly low one. This specific threshold was successfully applied in the study by Ren et al. [ 43 ], where they used this criterion, combined with an adjusted p-value &lt; 0.05, to identify 831 DEGs and construct a high-accuracy diagnostic model for ischemic stroke (AUC 0.81–0.933), thereby validating its reliability. In the current cardiorenal syndrome study, adopting this same threshold ensures comparability with published literature and helps focus on functionally relevant genes (e.g. those involved in inflammation and fibrosis pathways). This supports subsequent machine learning and pathway analyses, enhancing the study’s rigor and interpretability. 2.8.2. DALEX feature importance threshold: Top 20%
Selecting the top 20% of features based on importance scores calculated using the DALEXpackage is a widely adopted strategy in interpretable machine learning to balance model performance, complexity, and interpretability. DALEX uses permutation importance, where the contribution of each feature is estimated by measuring the drop in model performance (e.g. accuracy) when its values are randomly shuffled. A larger drop indicates greater feature importance. The top 20% cutoff enables the model to retain its most influential predictors while reducing data dimensionality, filtering out redundant or noisy variables, and improving both interpretability and computational efficiency. Relative importance ranking is generally more stable than absolute importance values, especially in high-dimensional

### 3.1. MR analysis of CKD and CAD
Using 891 stringently selected genetic IVs ( p &lt; 5 × 10 −8 , kb &gt; 10,000, and r 2 &lt; 0.001), MR analysis demonstrated that CKD is associated with an elevated risk of CAD (OR = 1.04, 95% CI: 1.033–1.047) ( Figure 2(A) ). Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of the causal inference, indicating no heterogeneity (Q test, p = 1.000), no evidence of horizontal pleiotropy (MR-Egger intercept, p = 0.750), and a well-supported causal directionality (Steiger test, p &lt; 1 × 10–15). In contrast, reverse MR analysis, conducted using 126 harmonized SNPs, showed no evidence of a causal effect of CAD on CKD (OR = 0.999, 95% CI: 0.962–1.037) ( Figure 2(B) ). All supporting figures and tables are available in the supplementary materials (Figure S1; Table S2 ).

### 3.2. Shared DEGs between CKD and CAD
Differential expression analysis of CAD versus CTL samples identified 7,326 DEGs based on thresholds of p &lt; 0.05 and |log 2 FC| &gt; 0.263 [ 43 ]. Among these, 3,404 genes were upregulated, and 3,922 were downregulated in CAD ( Figure 3(A,B) ). Similarly, comparison between CKD and CTL samples yielded 6,095 DEGs, including 4,709 upregulated and 1,386 downregulated genes ( Figure 3(C,D) ). Intersection analysis of upregulated and downregulated DEGs across both diseases identified 3,906 shared DEGs, suggesting overlapping molecular signatures that may underlie the comorbidity of CKD and CAD ( Figure 3(E) ).

### 3.3. MR analysis of shared plasma protein pQTLs and CAD
By intersecting the plasma proteins corresponding to the shared DEGs, a total of 230 proteins related to CKD–CAD comorbidity were identified ( Figure 4(A) ). A total of 9,053 SNPs were selected based on pQTL data from the DECODE database ( p &lt; 5 × 10 −8 , kb &gt; 10,000, and r 2 &lt; 0.001). After harmonization using the harmonise_data function, 5,864 valid IVs were retained. MR analysis identified 25 plasma proteins with a genetically causal association with CAD ( Figure 4(B,C) ). After sensitivity analysis, 15 proteins were retained as genetically causal candidates for CAD ( Figure 4(B,C) ). The robustness of these causal associations was supported by sensitivity analyses, which revealed no evidence of heterogeneity (Q test, p &gt; 0.05), no horizontal pleiotropy (MR-Egger intercept and MR-PRESSO global test, p &gt; 0.05), and strong support for causal directionality based on the Steiger test ( p &lt; 1 × 10 −10 ) ( Table 2 ). Furthermore, the scatter plot showed intercepts of IVs close to zero, and the funnel plot appeared symmetric without outliers, indicating minimal bias among the instruments ( Figure 4(D) ; Supplemental Figs. S2–S26 ).
Venn and forest plots identifying 15 CAD-linked proteins via pQTL-MR, plus funnel plots for sensitivity analysis. Table 2.
Mendelian randomization estimates identifying plasma proteins genetically causally linked to coronary artery disease in CKD–CAD comorbidity.

### 3.4. Functional enrichment analysis and PPI network of core proteins
GO enrichment analysis revealed that the 15 proteins were significantly associated with 208 functional terms (FDR &lt; 0.05), including 174 under the biological process category. Key enriched terms included the regulation of the smoothened signaling pathway ( Figure 5(A–D) ; Supplemental Figs. S27 –29). KEGG pathway analysis further revealed that these proteins were collectively involved in seven critical signaling pathways ( Figure 5(E) ; Figure S30; Table S3 ). PPI analysis, performed using a confidence threshold of 0.1, identified interaction pairs among 10 of the 15 proteins. The resulting interaction network, visualized using Cytoscape (version 3.8.2) ( Figure 5(F) ), highlighted HGF and SERPINE2 as nodes with the highest degree centrality, underscoring their potential regulatory importance within the network. Functional annotation showed that these proteins were predominantly enriched in signaling pathways associated with organ development and pathophysiological processes involving coagulation and fibrosis. Notably, the HGF-SERPINE2 interaction hub appeared to serve as a central mediator in the progression of cardiorenal fibrosis. Overall, the enriched pathways were organized into two major functional clusters: (1) developmental pathways involved in angiogenesis and tissue morphogenesis, and (2) pathological pathways associated with thrombosis, inflammatory responses, and fibrotic remodeling.

### 3.5. Selection and evaluation of diagnostic proteins
Candidate diagnostic proteins were identified via cross-validation using the Boruta algorithm and an SVM model with a radial basis function (SVM-RBF) in independent CAD and CKD cohorts ( Figure 6 ). A five-fold cross-validation strategy was employed, wherein the dataset was randomly divided into five equal subsets. During each iteration, four subsets were used for model training and one for validation, such that each subset served once as the validation set. The final performance was calculated as the average of all five validation results. Based on this strategy, six robust diagnostic biomarkers were identified: LIMA1, PLCG1, HGF, PZP, SERPINE2, and TXNDC15. Based on its suboptimal performance (AUC = 0.685, below the 0.7 threshold) in the CAD cohort, SPINT2 was excluded from the final diagnostic panel. This decision was based strictly on the pre-defined performance threshold. In the CAD cohort, the AUC values of the selected proteins ranged from 0.759 (LIMA1, PLCG1, TXNDC15) to 0.804 (SERPINE2). In contrast, the CKD cohort demonstrated markedly higher predictive performance, with AUC values ranging from 0.887 (SERPINE2) to 0.995 (PLCG1), the latter indicating near-perfect diagnostic accuracy ( Table 4 ). A nomogram model constructed using these six biomarkers ( Figure 7 ) enabled quantitative estimation of disease risk. For instance, a total score of 392 corresponded to a 99.9% probability of CAD, whereas a score of 305 corresponded to an approximately 100% probability of CKD. This model offers a clinically applicable tool for visualizing individual risk and facilitating early diagnosis.

### 3.6. MR analysis of CKD–diagnostic protein pQTLs
MR analysis demonstrated robust causal associations between genetically predicted CKD and six plasma diagnostic proteins: LIMA1 (OR = 1.065, 95% CI: 1.058–1.072), PZP (OR = 1.053, 95% CI: 1.046–1.061), and PLCG1 (OR = 1.046, 95% CI: 1.040–1.053) were identified as genetic risk factors for CAD; whereas SERPINE2 (OR = 0.99, 95% CI: 0.983–0.998), TXNDC15 (OR = 0.98, 95% CI: 0.973–0.986), and HGF (OR = 0.956, 95% CI: 0.950–0.960) acted as protective factors ( Figure 8(A) ). Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of these findings, indicating no significant heterogeneity (Cochran’s Q test, p &gt; 0.05), no evidence of horizontal pleiotropy (MR-Egger and MR-PRESSO tests, p &gt; 0.05), and no directional bias (Steiger test, p &lt; 1 × 10 −10 ). The validity of IVs was further supported by scatter plots and funnel plots ( Supplemental Figs. S31 –36; Table S4 ). Mediation analysis revealed that LIMA1, PZP, and PLCG1 mediated the positive causal effect of CKD on CAD, while HGF, SERPINE2, and TXNDC15 mediated protective effects, collectively constituting the causal pathway of “CKD–plasma protein–CAD” ( Figure 8(B) ; Table 3 ).

### 3.7. Construction of the GeneMANIA network and functional prediction of diagnostic proteins
A co-expression network comprising the six diagnostic proteins was generated using the GeneMANIA platform ( http://genemania.org/ ), which revealed significant interactions within pathways among these proteins ( Figure 9(A) ). Functional enrichment analysis showed that the diagnostic proteins and their interactors were collectively involved in biological processes such as regulation of cholesterol metabolic process, extrinsic component of plasma membrane, sterol biosynthetic process, host interaction, and regulation of alcohol/steroid biosynthetic processes ( Figure 9(B) ).
GeneMANIA network and function treemap of six core plasma proteins in sterol/lipid metabolism. GSEA further highlighted the regulation of several key biological pathways by these diagnostic proteins ( Figure 10 ; Supplemental Figs. S37–38 ).

### 3.8. ssGSEA of immune infiltration and diagnostic proteins
The ssGSEA of immune infiltration revealed distinct immune landscape alterations in both CAD and CKD. In CAD, seven pro-inflammatory immune cell populations, including dendritic cells (DCs), macrophages, and neutrophils, exhibited significantly increased infiltration scores ( p &lt; 0.01), whereas ten lymphocyte subsets, such as CD8 + T cells and cytotoxic cells, showed decreased infiltration scores ( Figure 11(A) . In contrast, the CKD cohort showed significantly decreased infiltration scores in twelve immune cell types, including cytotoxic cells and natural killer (NK) cells ( Figure 11(B) . Correlation analysis between key diagnostic proteins and immune cell abundance indicated disease-specific immune associations. Within the CAD microenvironment, HGF expression correlated positively with macrophages and neutrophils ( r &gt; 0.5) and negatively with CD8 + T cells (r &lt; −0.4); PLCG1 correlated positively with CD8 + T cells ( r = 0.42) and negatively with DCs (r = −0.38); PZP showed a significant negative correlation with macrophages (r = −0.61) ( Figures 11C ; Supplemental Figs. S39 –44). Within the CKD microenvironment, HGF, LIMA1, and SERPINE2 were negatively correlated with NK cells (r &lt; −0.6), while PZP correlated positively with effector memory T cells (Tem) ( r = 0.53) ( Figs 11D ; Supplemental Figs. S45 –50).

### 3.9. Drug–protein interaction prediction and molecular docking of diagnostic proteins
Potential drug–protein interactions were predicted using the DGIdb, which identified multiple drugs targeting HGF, PLCG1, and PZP ( Table 5 , Figure 12(A) ). Among these, compounds with the highest “interaction_group_score” were selected for molecular docking analyses. The three-dimensional crystal structures of the proteins and the corresponding small-molecule ligands were obtained for docking simulations ( Table 6 ). The docking results demonstrated stable interactions between the selected compounds and their protein targets. In HGF, three amino acid residues—TYR-369, ARG-331, and SER-378—formed hydrogen bonds with imatinib mesylate, yielding a docking affinity of −9.7 kcal/mol ( Figure 12(B) ). In PLCG1, three residues (GLN-659, GLU-548, SER-665) formed hydrogen bonds with phosphomethylphosphonic acid adenosyl ester, resulting in a docking affinity of −6.7 kcal/mol ( Figure 12(C) ). For PZP, two residues (SER-92, ASN-41) formed hydrogen bonds with norethindrone, with a docking affinity of −8.3 kcal/mol ( Figure 12(D) ). These docking interactions suggest that HGF, PLCG1, and PZP may serve as potential therapeutic targets for pharmacological modulation in cardiorenal comorbidity, warranting further experimental validation.

### 4.1. Background and pathogenic mechanisms of the lipid-inflammation axis
Recent advances in microarray and high-throughput sequencing technologies have markedly enhanced the understanding of molecular features and pathogenic mechanisms underlying complex diseases [ 46 , 47 ]. Meanwhile, the integration of bioinformatics with machine learning has become an increasingly powerful strategy for identifying novel pathogenic genes, diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers, elucidating disease mechanisms, and guiding targeted therapeutic development [ 48 , 49 ].
The lipid-inflammation axis serves as a critical bridge in the comorbidity of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and coronary artery disease (CAD). This bidirectional pathogenic loop arises from the interplay between lipid metabolism disorders and chronic inflammation, which together exacerbate cardiorenal injury. In CKD, impaired renal function leads to defective lipid clearance, causing elevated triglycerides, reduced high-density lipoprotein (HDL) levels, and accumulation of atherogenic low-density lipoprotein (LDL) particles [ 50 ]. These dyslipidemic changes promote lipid deposition in renal and vascular tissues, triggering lipotoxic injury and macrophage activation, with subsequent overproduction of inflammatory mediators like IL-6 and TNF-α [ 51 ]. Inflammation further amplifies lipid abnormalities by impairing lipoprotein metabolism and increasing oxidized lipid species [ 52 ]. Clinical evidence highlights biomarkers such as oxidized LDL and hs-CRP for early risk identification [ 53 ]. Therapeutic strategies like statins, which combine lipid-lowering and anti-inflammatory effects, target this axis [ 54 ]. CAD exacerbates the pathology through ischemia-induced hypoxia, activating RAAS and sympathetic pathways, which promote vasoconstriction and oxidative stress, advancing renal fibrosis and atherosclerosis [ 55 ]. This creates a positive feedback loop, where CAD-related hypoxia worsens lipid-inflammation dysregulation, accelerating CKD progression [ 56 ]. Thus, the axis integrates hemodynam

### 4.3. Clinical implications and therapeutic potential
The clinical management of CAD in patients with CKD has long been constrained by diagnostic and therapeutic limitations. Diagnostic approaches have traditionally relied on single indicators—such as eGFR to assess renal function or coronary artery calcium scoring to evaluate vascular lesions [ 57 ], while treatment strategies have primarily focused on non-organ-specific interventions, such as lipid-lowering statins [ 58 ]. This compartmentalized approach overlooks the shared pathophysiological mechanisms underpinning cardiorenal interactions, leading to inadequate risk stratification and delayed therapeutic intervention. Furthermore, therapeutic choices remain limited for patients with advanced CKD, who are frequently excluded from major cardiovascular outcome trials. As a result, cardiovascular management in CKD is often extrapolated from non-CKD populations, diminishing its clinical applicability [ 59 ]. By integrating transcriptomic and plasma proteomic genetic data, this study provides a novel MR-validated multi-protein biomarker signature involving a six-protein panel (LIMA1, PLCG1, HGF, PZP, SERPINE2, and TXNDC15) with robust diagnostic potential. Machine learning–based feature selection validated its strong discriminative capacity in both CAD (AUC = 0.759–0.804) and CKD (AUC = 0.887–0.995) cohorts. This plasma protein panel represents a shift from isolated organ assessment toward a coordinated, multi-target diagnostic strategy. The use of quantifiable circulating biomarkers offers a more comprehensive and biologically grounded approach for the early identification of individuals at high risk of developing cardiorenal comorbidity.
Dyslipidemia has long been recognized as a shared risk factor for both CAD and CKD [ 60 ]. Therapeutic strategies targeting lipid metabolism have dual benefits in cardiorenal comorbidities: statins not only reduce the risk of cardiovascular events in CKD patients but also improve renal function [ 61 ]; combination therapy with statins

### 4.4. The regulatory role of macrophage polarization and immune microenvironment in cardiorenal comorbidity
For decades, macrophage polarization has been recognized as a key determinant in the pathogenesis of both CKD and CAD. In CKD, infiltrating M1-type macrophages promote renal interstitial fibrosis by releasing pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-1β, while M2-type macrophages contribute to tissue repair—an established concept supported by numerous studies [ 66 , 67 ]. Similarly, earlier studies on CAD have reported highly similar mechanisms, suggesting that macrophage dysfunction may disrupt immune tolerance in CAD patients, thereby accelerating disease progression. Modulating macrophage polarization from the pro-inflammatory M1 phenotype to the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype has been shown to improve cardiovascular health and mitigate the development of atherosclerosis [ 68 ]. This cross-organ paradigm of macrophage polarization thus provides mechanistic support for the proposed “cardiorenal lipid-inflammation axis.” In this study, immune infiltration analysis revealed potential protein-mediated modulation of macrophage functional plasticity. In the CAD group ( Figure 11(A /C)), macrophage infiltration scores were significantly increased and positively correlated with HGF, SERPINE2, and TXNDC15 ( r &gt; 0), suggesting that these proteins may promote macrophage activation. Conversely, macrophage scores exhibited significant negative correlations with PLCG1 and PZP ( r &lt; 0), implying suppressive effects on macrophage activity.

### 4.5. Mechanisms and therapeutic implications of core plasma proteins mediating cardiorenal comorbidity via modulation of the lipid-inflammation axis
Notably, the known role of LIMA1 in intestinal cholesterol absorption [ 76 ] aligns with our findings on its regulatory function in lipid metabolism, thus further supporting the central role of lipid dysregulation in cardiorenal disease. Based on these insights, we propose that targeting the lipid–inflammation axis (for instance, modulating LIMA1-mediated cholesterol metabolism) may serve as a novel therapeutic strategy for simultaneously mitigating cardiac and renal injury. This approach not only builds on the established clinical benefits of lipid-lowering therapy but also provides a mechanistic foundation for the development of precision-targeted interventions in cardiorenal syndrome.
As a multi-domain protein activated through proteolytic cleavage, HGF regulates critical processes, including cell migration, proliferation, and apoptosis. In response to tissue injury, upregulated HGF expression activates anti-apoptotic pathways, promotes angiogenesis, and enhances the secretion of the anti-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-10 (IL-10). Upon binding to its receptor Met, HGF exerts cardioprotective effects by inhibiting hypoxia-induced autophagy and has been identified as a potential biomarker for cardiovascular diseases [ 77–79 ]. In this study, MR analysis confirmed that HGF may serve as an endogenous protective factor that mitigates both renal and cardiovascular injury. GSEA revealed significant activation of lysosomal function and autophagy regulatory pathways in CAD patients with high HGF expression ( Figure 10(a) ). These results are consistent with previous reports demonstrating that HGF prevents autophagic cell death and maintains cardiomyocyte homeostasis via the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway [ 80 ]. Remarkably, this study uncovers a novel bidirectional regulatory role of HGF in the cardiorenal system. In the CKD cohort, HGF significantly activated ferroptosis pathways ( Figure 10(b) ), which could be interpreted as evidence of a potential link to lipid peroxid

### 4.6. Methodological comparison and positioning: the relationship between this study and previous Mendelian randomization-machine learning research in the field of cardiorenal disease
The research paradigm integrating Mendelian randomization and machine learning employed in this study is highly consistent with recent trends in biomarker discovery for cardiovascular and renal diseases published in top-tier international journals, while providing distinctive refinement for the complex disease model of cardiorenal comorbidity. For instance, a landmark 2024 study published in European Heart Journal (IF = 37.6) systematically analyzed the associations between 259 plasma proteins and myocardial infarction (MI) risk using large-scale cohorts and a two-sample MR approach, successfully identifying 45 associated proteins and specifically revealing significant sex-specific differences in 13 of them, with stronger associations in women [ 94 ]. Furthermore, a systematic study published in Protein &amp; Cell (IF = 12.8) in 2025 analyzed 14-year follow-up data from 53,026 participants, linked 2,920 plasma proteins to 14 cardiovascular disease outcomes, and through machine learning models and two-sample MR analysis, not only screened high-performance predictive biomarkers but also validated their causal relationship with the diseases, providing crucial evidence for precise early warning [ 95 ]. In the field of kidney disease, a study published in Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism (IF = 5.7) integrated machine learning, MR, and mediation analysis to successfully pinpoint key genes for diabetic kidney disease and elucidated their mechanism of influencing disease progression by regulating pathways such as renal fibrosis and inflammation, demonstrating the depth of this method in deciphering complex kidney pathologies [ 96 ].

### 4.7. Novelty and future applications
The core innovation of this study lies in the identification and validation of a specific combination of six proteins, which may provide a precise tool for risk assessment of cardiorenal comorbidity that is potentially superior to traditional clinical indicators [ 97 ]. At the translational application level, this protein signature can be further developed as a key component of a polygenic risk scoring system; research indicates that integrating proteomic information with genetic risk data can significantly enhance the identification of high-risk populations for cardiovascular events and renal function progression [ 98–99 ]. A dynamic risk stratification model constructed based on this score could enable precise recommendations for personalized screening initiation times and monitoring frequencies for patients at different risk levels, thereby optimizing the allocation of clinical resources [ 100 ]. More importantly, as key mediators of specific pathophysiological pathways, these proteins can be directly incorporated into drug screening pipelines. For instance, levels of proteins such as hepatocyte growth factor are significantly associated with cardiovascular mortality risk, providing direction for rapidly identifying candidate compounds that can modulate these targets and opening new avenues for developing targeted therapies and individualized treatment strategies for cardiorenal comorbidity [ 101 ].

### 1. Introduction
Chronic kidney disease (CKD), a major global health burden, is defined as kidney damage or a glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 for three months or more, irrespective of cause [ 1 ]. It is characterized by a progressive decline in kidney function, leading to the accumulation of toxins and metabolic waste in the body, and may ultimately progress to end-stage renal disease (ESRD). According to epidemiological data, the global prevalence of CKD is approximately 9.5% [ 2 ]. Mounting evidence indicates that CKD is associated not only with impaired renal filtration but also with abnormal lipid metabolism, activation of inflammatory pathways, and elevated oxidative stress [ 3–5 ]. Consequently, patients with CKD frequently develop coronary artery disease (CAD), a narrowing or blockage of the coronary arteries, typically due to the buildup of plaque [ 6 ], which results in a markedly increased risk of cardiovascular events, particularly among those with advanced renal impairment. The mortality from heart disease is substantially higher in individuals with CKD than in those without renal dysfunction [ 7 ]. Moreover, CKD is recognized as an independent predictor of poor prognosis in CAD [ 8 ], while CAD, primarily caused by atherosclerosis of the coronary arteries, leads to myocardial ischemia and is a major contributor to myocardial infarction and heart failure. Studies have identified CAD as the leading single cause of death worldwide [ 9 ]. The high comorbidity rate and the complex, bidirectional interactions between these two diseases are particularly noteworthy [ 10 ]. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying CKD-CAD comorbidity remain complex and incompletely understood. Thus, investigating the pathogenic link between CKD and CAD holds substantial clinical significance. Against this backdrop, artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) technologies offer powerful tools for deciphering the complex mechanisms underlying CKD-CAD c

### 2.1. Experimental design and data sources
The GWAS summary statistics for CKD were obtained from the CKDGen consortium ( https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gwas/ ), comprising a sample of 452,264 individuals of European ancestry [ 23 ]. The chronic kidney disease (CKD) GWAS summary statistics were obtained from the CKDGen consortium, which primarily includes individuals with mild to moderate CKD stages and explicitly excludes end-stage renal disease (ESRD) or dialysis patients. Summary-level data for coronary artery disease (CAD) were retrieved from the IEU Open GWAS database ( https://gwas.mrcieu.ac.uk ), accession number ebi-a-GCST005195, comprising 122,733 CAD cases and 424,528 controls [ 24 ]. This case includes a composite endpoint of myocardial infarction, stable or unstable angina, and significant stenosis confirmed by coronary angiography. In addition, cis-pQTLs were defined as single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) located within 1 Mb of the gene encoding the corresponding plasma protein. The pQTL dataset was derived from the DECODE database ( https://www.decode.com/ ) based on the 2021 study by Ferkingstad et al. which included 35,559 participants and quantified 4907 plasma proteins [ 25 ]. Gene expression data were downloaded from the GEO database. GSE113079 ( https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE113079 ) contained blood microarray data from 93 patients with CAD and 48 healthy controls (CTLs), generated using the GPL20115 platform. GSE66494 ( https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE66494 ) included blood microarray data from 53 patients with CKD and 8 CTLs, profiled on the GPL6480 platform ( https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/ ) [ 26 ] ( Table 1 , Supplemental Table S1 ).

### 2.8. Justification for threshold selection methods in the analysis
2.8.1. Differentially Expressed Gene (DEG) cutoff: |log 2 FC| &gt; 0.263
The threshold of |log 2 FC| &gt; 0.263 (corresponding to a |FC| ≥ 1.2) for screening differentially expressed genes (DEGs) was selected based on biological rationale and field consensus. This cutoff aims to balance sensitivity and specificity, enabling the capture of subtle yet stable expression changes while avoiding the omission of key signals with an overly high threshold or the introduction of noise with an overly low one. This specific threshold was successfully applied in the study by Ren et al. [ 43 ], where they used this criterion, combined with an adjusted p-value &lt; 0.05, to identify 831 DEGs and construct a high-accuracy diagnostic model for ischemic stroke (AUC 0.81–0.933), thereby validating its reliability. In the current cardiorenal syndrome study, adopting this same threshold ensures comparability with published literature and helps focus on functionally relevant genes (e.g. those involved in inflammation and fibrosis pathways). This supports subsequent machine learning and pathway analyses, enhancing the study’s rigor and interpretability. 2.8.2. DALEX feature importance threshold: Top 20%
Selecting the top 20% of features based on importance scores calculated using the DALEXpackage is a widely adopted strategy in interpretable machine learning to balance model performance, complexity, and interpretability. DALEX uses permutation importance, where the contribution of each feature is estimated by measuring the drop in model performance (e.g. accuracy) when its values are randomly shuffled. A larger drop indicates greater feature importance. The top 20% cutoff enables the model to retain its most influential predictors while reducing data dimensionality, filtering out redundant or noisy variables, and improving both interpretability and computational efficiency. Relative importance ranking is generally more stable than absolute importance values, especially in high-dimensional

### 3.1. MR analysis of CKD and CAD
Using 891 stringently selected genetic IVs ( p &lt; 5 × 10 −8 , kb &gt; 10,000, and r 2 &lt; 0.001), MR analysis demonstrated that CKD is associated with an elevated risk of CAD (OR = 1.04, 95% CI: 1.033–1.047) ( Figure 2(A) ). Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of the causal inference, indicating no heterogeneity (Q test, p = 1.000), no evidence of horizontal pleiotropy (MR-Egger intercept, p = 0.750), and a well-supported causal directionality (Steiger test, p &lt; 1 × 10–15). In contrast, reverse MR analysis, conducted using 126 harmonized SNPs, showed no evidence of a causal effect of CAD on CKD (OR = 0.999, 95% CI: 0.962–1.037) ( Figure 2(B) ). All supporting figures and tables are available in the supplementary materials (Figure S1; Table S2 ).

### 3.2. Shared DEGs between CKD and CAD
Differential expression analysis of CAD versus CTL samples identified 7,326 DEGs based on thresholds of p &lt; 0.05 and |log 2 FC| &gt; 0.263 [ 43 ]. Among these, 3,404 genes were upregulated, and 3,922 were downregulated in CAD ( Figure 3(A,B) ). Similarly, comparison between CKD and CTL samples yielded 6,095 DEGs, including 4,709 upregulated and 1,386 downregulated genes ( Figure 3(C,D) ). Intersection analysis of upregulated and downregulated DEGs across both diseases identified 3,906 shared DEGs, suggesting overlapping molecular signatures that may underlie the comorbidity of CKD and CAD ( Figure 3(E) ).

### 3.3. MR analysis of shared plasma protein pQTLs and CAD
By intersecting the plasma proteins corresponding to the shared DEGs, a total of 230 proteins related to CKD–CAD comorbidity were identified ( Figure 4(A) ). A total of 9,053 SNPs were selected based on pQTL data from the DECODE database ( p &lt; 5 × 10 −8 , kb &gt; 10,000, and r 2 &lt; 0.001). After harmonization using the harmonise_data function, 5,864 valid IVs were retained. MR analysis identified 25 plasma proteins with a genetically causal association with CAD ( Figure 4(B,C) ). After sensitivity analysis, 15 proteins were retained as genetically causal candidates for CAD ( Figure 4(B,C) ). The robustness of these causal associations was supported by sensitivity analyses, which revealed no evidence of heterogeneity (Q test, p &gt; 0.05), no horizontal pleiotropy (MR-Egger intercept and MR-PRESSO global test, p &gt; 0.05), and strong support for causal directionality based on the Steiger test ( p &lt; 1 × 10 −10 ) ( Table 2 ). Furthermore, the scatter plot showed intercepts of IVs close to zero, and the funnel plot appeared symmetric without outliers, indicating minimal bias among the instruments ( Figure 4(D) ; Supplemental Figs. S2–S26 ).
Venn and forest plots identifying 15 CAD-linked proteins via pQTL-MR, plus funnel plots for sensitivity analysis. Table 2.
Mendelian randomization estimates identifying plasma proteins genetically causally linked to coronary artery disease in CKD–CAD comorbidity.

### 3.4. Functional enrichment analysis and PPI network of core proteins
GO enrichment analysis revealed that the 15 proteins were significantly associated with 208 functional terms (FDR &lt; 0.05), including 174 under the biological process category. Key enriched terms included the regulation of the smoothened signaling pathway ( Figure 5(A–D) ; Supplemental Figs. S27 –29). KEGG pathway analysis further revealed that these proteins were collectively involved in seven critical signaling pathways ( Figure 5(E) ; Figure S30; Table S3 ). PPI analysis, performed using a confidence threshold of 0.1, identified interaction pairs among 10 of the 15 proteins. The resulting interaction network, visualized using Cytoscape (version 3.8.2) ( Figure 5(F) ), highlighted HGF and SERPINE2 as nodes with the highest degree centrality, underscoring their potential regulatory importance within the network. Functional annotation showed that these proteins were predominantly enriched in signaling pathways associated with organ development and pathophysiological processes involving coagulation and fibrosis. Notably, the HGF-SERPINE2 interaction hub appeared to serve as a central mediator in the progression of cardiorenal fibrosis. Overall, the enriched pathways were organized into two major functional clusters: (1) developmental pathways involved in angiogenesis and tissue morphogenesis, and (2) pathological pathways associated with thrombosis, inflammatory responses, and fibrotic remodeling.

### 3.5. Selection and evaluation of diagnostic proteins
Candidate diagnostic proteins were identified via cross-validation using the Boruta algorithm and an SVM model with a radial basis function (SVM-RBF) in independent CAD and CKD cohorts ( Figure 6 ). A five-fold cross-validation strategy was employed, wherein the dataset was randomly divided into five equal subsets. During each iteration, four subsets were used for model training and one for validation, such that each subset served once as the validation set. The final performance was calculated as the average of all five validation results. Based on this strategy, six robust diagnostic biomarkers were identified: LIMA1, PLCG1, HGF, PZP, SERPINE2, and TXNDC15. Based on its suboptimal performance (AUC = 0.685, below the 0.7 threshold) in the CAD cohort, SPINT2 was excluded from the final diagnostic panel. This decision was based strictly on the pre-defined performance threshold. In the CAD cohort, the AUC values of the selected proteins ranged from 0.759 (LIMA1, PLCG1, TXNDC15) to 0.804 (SERPINE2). In contrast, the CKD cohort demonstrated markedly higher predictive performance, with AUC values ranging from 0.887 (SERPINE2) to 0.995 (PLCG1), the latter indicating near-perfect diagnostic accuracy ( Table 4 ). A nomogram model constructed using these six biomarkers ( Figure 7 ) enabled quantitative estimation of disease risk. For instance, a total score of 392 corresponded to a 99.9% probability of CAD, whereas a score of 305 corresponded to an approximately 100% probability of CKD. This model offers a clinically applicable tool for visualizing individual risk and facilitating early diagnosis.
ML selection of six plasma biomarkers for CKD–CAD diagnosis using Boruta and SVM-RBF. Table 4.

### 3.6. MR analysis of CKD–diagnostic protein pQTLs
MR analysis demonstrated robust causal associations between genetically predicted CKD and six plasma diagnostic proteins: LIMA1 (OR = 1.065, 95% CI: 1.058–1.072), PZP (OR = 1.053, 95% CI: 1.046–1.061), and PLCG1 (OR = 1.046, 95% CI: 1.040–1.053) were identified as genetic risk factors for CAD; whereas SERPINE2 (OR = 0.99, 95% CI: 0.983–0.998), TXNDC15 (OR = 0.98, 95% CI: 0.973–0.986), and HGF (OR = 0.956, 95% CI: 0.950–0.960) acted as protective factors ( Figure 8(A) ). Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of these findings, indicating no significant heterogeneity (Cochran’s Q test, p &gt; 0.05), no evidence of horizontal pleiotropy (MR-Egger and MR-PRESSO tests, p &gt; 0.05), and no directional bias (Steiger test, p &lt; 1 × 10 −10 ). The validity of IVs was further supported by scatter plots and funnel plots ( Supplemental Figs. S31 –36; Table S4 ). Mediation analysis revealed that LIMA1, PZP, and PLCG1 mediated the positive causal effect of CKD on CAD, while HGF, SERPINE2, and TXNDC15 mediated protective effects, collectively constituting the causal pathway of “CKD–plasma protein–CAD” ( Figure 8(B) ; Table 3 ).

### 3.7. Construction of the GeneMANIA network and functional prediction of diagnostic proteins
A co-expression network comprising the six diagnostic proteins was generated using the GeneMANIA platform ( http://genemania.org/ ), which revealed significant interactions within pathways among these proteins ( Figure 9(A) ). Functional enrichment analysis showed that the diagnostic proteins and their interactors were collectively involved in biological processes such as regulation of cholesterol metabolic process, extrinsic component of plasma membrane, sterol biosynthetic process, host interaction, and regulation of alcohol/steroid biosynthetic processes ( Figure 9(B) ).
GeneMANIA network and function treemap of six core plasma proteins in sterol/lipid metabolism. GSEA further highlighted the regulation of several key biological pathways by these diagnostic proteins ( Figure 10 ; Supplemental Figs. S37–38 ).

### 3.8. ssGSEA of immune infiltration and diagnostic proteins
The ssGSEA of immune infiltration revealed distinct immune landscape alterations in both CAD and CKD. In CAD, seven pro-inflammatory immune cell populations, including dendritic cells (DCs), macrophages, and neutrophils, exhibited significantly increased infiltration scores ( p &lt; 0.01), whereas ten lymphocyte subsets, such as CD8 + T cells and cytotoxic cells, showed decreased infiltration scores ( Figure 11(A) . In contrast, the CKD cohort showed significantly decreased infiltration scores in twelve immune cell types, including cytotoxic cells and natural killer (NK) cells ( Figure 11(B) . Correlation analysis between key diagnostic proteins and immune cell abundance indicated disease-specific immune associations. Within the CAD microenvironment, HGF expression correlated positively with macrophages and neutrophils ( r &gt; 0.5) and negatively with CD8 + T cells (r &lt; −0.4); PLCG1 correlated positively with CD8 + T cells ( r = 0.42) and negatively with DCs (r = −0.38); PZP showed a significant negative correlation with macrophages (r = −0.61) ( Figures 11C ; Supplemental Figs. S39 –44). Within the CKD microenvironment, HGF, LIMA1, and SERPINE2 were negatively correlated with NK cells (r &lt; −0.6), while PZP correlated positively with effector memory T cells (Tem) ( r = 0.53) ( Figs 11D ; Supplemental Figs. S45 –50).

### 3.9. Drug–protein interaction prediction and molecular docking of diagnostic proteins
Potential drug–protein interactions were predicted using the DGIdb, which identified multiple drugs targeting HGF, PLCG1, and PZP ( Table 5 , Figure 12(A) ). Among these, compounds with the highest “interaction_group_score” were selected for molecular docking analyses. The three-dimensional crystal structures of the proteins and the corresponding small-molecule ligands were obtained for docking simulations ( Table 6 ). The docking results demonstrated stable interactions between the selected compounds and their protein targets. In HGF, three amino acid residues—TYR-369, ARG-331, and SER-378—formed hydrogen bonds with imatinib mesylate, yielding a docking affinity of −9.7 kcal/mol ( Figure 12(B) ). In PLCG1, three residues (GLN-659, GLU-548, SER-665) formed hydrogen bonds with phosphomethylphosphonic acid adenosyl ester, resulting in a docking affinity of −6.7 kcal/mol ( Figure 12(C) ). For PZP, two residues (SER-92, ASN-41) formed hydrogen bonds with norethindrone, with a docking affinity of −8.3 kcal/mol ( Figure 12(D) ). These docking interactions suggest that HGF, PLCG1, and PZP may serve as potential therapeutic targets for pharmacological modulation in cardiorenal comorbidity, warranting further experimental validation.
